items.title: L11: Anatomy of a HEO or SEO advert
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: An advert on Civil Service Jobs follows a recognisable structure, and each part answers a different question. The job summary and role description say what the post does and where it sits. The person specification, sometimes headed essential criteria or what we are looking for, sets out the Success Profile elements that will be assessed. The details section gives the grade, salary range, location, working pattern, contract type and number of posts. A section often headed things you need to know covers security clearance, nationality rules, pre-employment checks and whether the post is open to civil servants only. The how-to-apply section explains what you must submit, such as a CV, a personal statement or answers to questions, and the selection section lists the stages and the dates. A HEO or SEO advert normally expects you to show you can manage people or complex work, or at least lead small pieces of work, whereas an EO advert is more about delivering tasks accurately. Do not skim the details: the closing date is usually fixed, late applications are normally not accepted, and an advert that says it may close early if enough applications arrive means you should not wait. Read the advert against your own evidence before you apply, and note which criteria are marked as the ones scored at sift, because those decide whether you reach interview.

questions.prompt: Which part of a Civil Service Jobs advert tells you what the sift will actually score?

options.text: The person specification listing the Success Profile elements to be assessed
The benefits section explaining leave and pension arrangements for staff
The department summary describing its wider purpose, history and priorities
The details section giving grade, salary range and location of the post

questions.hint: The person specification names what is assessed.

questions.prompt: Where would you most likely find whether a post is restricted to existing civil servants?

options.text: In the salary range, which is set differently for internal candidates
In the things-you-need-to-know and eligibility information near the details
In the job title, which always includes the word internal for such posts
In the closing date line, which is earlier for civil servants than others

questions.hint: Eligibility and restrictions appear in the details and things-you-need-to-know sections.

questions.prompt: An advert says it may close early if enough applications arrive. What is the sensible response?

options.text: Wait until the final day so your evidence is as polished as possible
Treat the stated date as guaranteed because it is in the advert
Submit well before the stated closing date rather than waiting for it
Ask the team to confirm they will keep it open for your application

questions.hint: A stated early-closing possibility means the date is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: How does a HEO or SEO advert usually differ from an EO advert in what it expects?

options.text: It requires a degree as an essential criterion for every post
It places more weight on length of service in the grade directly below
It drops behaviours and assesses only technical qualifications
It places more weight on leading work or people and handling complexity

questions.hint: Higher grades are expected to lead and manage complexity.

questions.prompt: Which advert detail most directly decides whether you could practically accept an offer?

options.text: The name of the recruiting department's director
The number of other posts the department is filling
The date the advert was first published
Location, working pattern and contract type

questions.hint: Practical terms decide whether you can take the job.

questions.prompt: What does the how-to-apply section normally tell you?

options.text: Which Success Profile elements the previous post-holder had
How many candidates are expected to pass the sift
What you must submit and which stages and dates follow
What scores earlier applicants achieved at interview

questions.hint: It sets out application requirements and the timeline.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to apply without reading the security and eligibility information?

options.text: You could be ineligible or fail clearance after spending time applying
Sift panels automatically reject candidates who have not acknowledged it
Clearance is only reviewed once probation has been completed
Eligibility rules are only introduced once you reach interview

questions.hint: Eligibility and clearance rules can rule you out whatever your merit.

questions.prompt: A post lists six essential criteria and says only two will be scored at sift. What does this suggest?

options.text: Write equally about all six so the panel can choose which to score
Put your best evidence behind those two and prepare the rest later
Ignore the other four, since they will not be assessed at any stage
Leave those two for the interview and use the sift on the others

questions.hint: Sift scoring concentrates on the stated criteria; the rest are assessed later.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first step when an advert is unclear about the grade of the post?

options.text: Assume the grade is the one above what the salary range suggests
Contact the recruiting team named in the advert and ask
Apply anyway and raise the question if you reach interview
Compare with another department's advert carrying a similar title

questions.hint: The named contact is the right person to clarify.

questions.prompt: What does the selection section of an advert most usefully allow you to plan?

options.text: The salary point you will be placed at if you succeed
Which panel member will ask which question at the interview
Your preparation for each stage and any adjustments to request
The date by which you can expect an offer, which is binding

questions.hint: Stages and dates let you schedule preparation and adjustments.

items.title: L11: Role profile versus person specification
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: People often blur two documents that serve different purposes. The role profile, sometimes called the job description, describes the job: purpose, main responsibilities, reporting lines, budget or team size and the work that will be done day to day. The person specification describes the person: the behaviours, strengths, experience, technical skills and ability the post needs. When you apply, you are assessed against the person specification, not the job description. This matters because candidates who copy phrases from the role profile into their statement score badly: the panel wants evidence that you have the Success Profile elements, not a restatement of the duties. The role profile helps in other ways. It tells you the level of independence, the type of stakeholders and the complexity you would face, so you can judge whether your evidence is at the right scale. If the role profile mentions managing a team of operational staff and you have only coordinated a project, you can still apply, but you should use the evidence you do have honestly and explain how it would transfer. Equally, if the profile describes work well below what you do now, ask whether the move is a promotion in substance. A role profile that is vague about scope is a signal to ask the recruiting team questions before you apply. Treat the two documents together: the profile tells you what the job is, the specification tells you how you will be judged.

questions.prompt: Against which document are applicants primarily scored?

options.text: The role profile listing the main duties and reporting line of the post
The most recent appraisal of the previous post-holder
The department's published business plan for the coming year
The person specification setting out the Success Profile elements

questions.hint: Scoring is against the Success Profile elements in the person specification.

questions.prompt: What mistake do candidates make when they copy phrases from the role profile into their statement?

options.text: They restate duties instead of evidencing the behaviours required
They reveal that they have not yet been security cleared
They accidentally apply to a different post from the one advertised
They break copyright in the advert and risk being disqualified

questions.hint: Duties are not evidence of what you have done.

questions.prompt: What can the role profile tell you that helps you judge your own fit?

options.text: How the interview panel is likely to vote on each of your answers
The number of other candidates who are likely to apply for the post
The scale of responsibility, stakeholders and independence the post involves
The sift score that will be needed to reach the interview stage

questions.hint: It shows the complexity and scale, so you can compare your evidence.

questions.prompt: A role profile mentions managing a team of operational staff and you have led only a project team. What is the most sensible approach?

options.text: Apply, using your real leadership evidence and showing how it transfers
Apply only if the advert allows you to skip the leadership question
Hold off until you have formally line-managed a team of that kind
Describe your project team as an operational team to match the profile

questions.hint: Transferable evidence can be enough, but it must be honest.

questions.prompt: Your current duties resemble the role profile of a higher-graded advert. What is the right next question?

options.text: Whether your manager will backdate your pay to match the higher grade
Whether the salary range is wide enough to include your current pay
Whether your department will confirm you for promotion without competing
Whether you can show the higher grade's behaviours and scale

questions.hint: Similar tasks do not prove higher-grade capability.

questions.prompt: A role profile is vague about scope. What should you do before applying?

options.text: Fill the gaps with your own best guess about the post
Ask the recruiting contact about team size, budget and stakeholders
Assume the scope matches your current post and write on that basis
Apply and decline later if the scope turns out to be larger

questions.hint: The advert contact can clarify scope before you invest effort.

questions.prompt: What does the person specification generally contain?

options.text: The terms of the pension and leave entitlement that come with the post
The reporting line, team size and budget the post-holder will manage
A history of the post, including previous holders and why it fell vacant
The behaviours, strengths, experience, technical skills and ability being sought

questions.hint: It lists the Success Profile elements sought.

questions.prompt: Why might the role profile affect which example you choose for a sift answer?

options.text: Your example should reuse the profile's wording as far as possible
Your example should be of comparable scale and complexity to the post
Your example should come from outside work to avoid confidentiality issues
Your example should always be the most recent whatever its scale

questions.hint: Choose evidence at a similar scale and complexity.

questions.prompt: Which is the best reason to read both documents together?

options.text: The specification is optional reading once you have read the profile
They contain the same information presented in two formats
The profile shows the job and the specification shows the criteria
Only the profile is required by law to be accurate

questions.hint: Together they give the job and the criteria.

questions.prompt: An applicant spends most of a 750-word statement describing current duties. What is the likely result?

options.text: A low score, because duties are not evidence of behaviours and results
Automatic progression to interview since the duties match the profile
A request to add a CV so that the panel can see the actual results
A high score, because the length of experience is clearly shown by the duties

questions.hint: Panels score evidence of what you did and achieved.

items.title: L11: The five Success Profile elements
items.body: Success Profiles are the Civil Service framework for assessing candidates and describing roles. There are five elements. Behaviours are the actions and activities that people do which result in effective performance in a job, drawn from the Civil Service Behaviours such as Seeing the Big Picture, Making Effective Decisions, Communicating and Influencing, Working Together, Developing Self and Others, Managing a Quality Service, Delivering at Pace, Changing and Improving, and Leadership. Strengths are the things a person does regularly, does well and is energised by. Ability is the aptitude or potential to learn, for example through numerical or verbal reasoning tests. Technical covers the specific professional skills or qualifications a job needs, such as an accountancy qualification or a recognised project management standard. Experience covers the knowledge or mastery of an activity or subject gained through education, a career or other life experience. A recruiter does not have to assess all five elements. The advert normally says which are used, because assessing too many can disadvantage candidates and lengthen the process. The framework allows a mix of elements across the stages, so you may meet strengths at interview, behaviours in a written sift and ability in an online test. For an applicant, the practical lesson is to read which elements the advert names and prepare evidence for each, rather than preparing generic answers.

questions.prompt: How many elements make up Success Profiles?

options.text: Six
Five
Three
Four

questions.hint: Behaviours, strengths, ability, technical and experience.

questions.prompt: Which element is measured by tests such as numerical or verbal reasoning?

options.text: Ability
Experience
Behaviours
Strengths

questions.hint: Aptitude and potential are assessed as ability.

questions.prompt: Which element best describes the things a person does regularly, does well and enjoys?

options.text: Behaviours
Technical
Ability
Strengths

questions.hint: That is the definition of strengths.

questions.prompt: A post requires a recognised accountancy qualification. Which element does this fall under?

options.text: Ability
Behaviours
Technical
Strengths

questions.hint: Professional qualifications and skills are technical.

questions.prompt: Must every vacancy assess all five Success Profile elements?

options.text: Only senior grade vacancies are permitted to assess fewer than five
Every vacancy must assess all five or the competition is unlawful
Recruiters choose a suitable mix and the advert names the ones used
Only external competitions are permitted to assess fewer than five

questions.hint: Recruiters select the elements relevant to the role.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the Civil Service Behaviours?

options.text: Rapid Response
Corporate Loyalty
Independent Initiative
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Delivering at Pace is a listed behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why do recruiters avoid assessing too many elements?

options.text: It can lengthen the process and disadvantage candidates unnecessarily
Candidates are said to dislike structured assessment formats
The law caps assessment at two elements for any single vacancy
Panels are unable to score more than one element at the same time

questions.hint: Selection should be proportionate to the role.

questions.prompt: Which element covers knowledge gained through education, a career or other life experience?

options.text: Ability
Experience
Strengths
Technical

questions.hint: Experience covers what you have done and know.

questions.prompt: An advert says behaviours are assessed in writing and strengths at interview. How should you prepare?

options.text: Prepare only strengths answers, as they cover the whole process
Prepare the technical qualifications for the interview instead
Prepare one set of answers designed to serve both stages
Behaviour evidence in writing now and strengths answers for interview

questions.hint: Prepare each element for its own stage.

questions.prompt: Which description best separates behaviours from strengths?

options.text: Behaviours apply to junior grades only, whereas strengths are used at senior grades
They mean the same thing but appear on different forms and are scored separately
Behaviours are actions that bring effective performance, strengths are what you do well and enjoy
Behaviours are fixed from birth, whereas strengths are learned at work and measured by tests

questions.hint: Behaviours are performance actions, strengths are energising talents.

items.title: L11: Behaviour levels by grade
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: Each Civil Service Behaviour is described at several levels, so that the same behaviour is expected differently at different grades. The levels broadly map to groups of grades: the lowest level suits roles such as AA and AO, the next level suits EO, the third level usually covers HEO and SEO, and the fourth level usually covers Grade 7 and Grade 6. Senior Civil Service roles use higher levels again. This is a general pattern, and the advert names the level that applies to the post, so check it rather than assuming. The levels describe both scope and independence. At a lower level, Making Effective Decisions might involve using information to make routine choices within guidelines. At a higher level it involves weighing complex or incomplete evidence, balancing risk and judging when to escalate, with consequences that affect others. The same pattern applies to Leadership: at HEO and SEO it is about leading a team or piece of work, setting direction and developing others, while at Grade 7 it extends to leading through other managers or across teams. When you write evidence, aim at the level of the post, not above or below. Evidence from a level below can make you look unready, and claiming evidence from a level above without having done it can fail at interview. If you have little at the target level, find stretch opportunities.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour level normally applies to both HEO and SEO posts?

options.text: The third level
The fifth level
The first level
The second level

questions.hint: HEO and SEO usually share a level.

questions.prompt: Where should you check which behaviour level applies to a post?

options.text: In the text of the Civil Service Code on values
In the advert, which names the level assessed
In your own most recent appraisal and objectives
In the department's published pay scale for the grade

questions.hint: The advert states the level being assessed.

questions.prompt: What do the behaviour levels chiefly describe?

options.text: The salary range attached to each group of grades
The number of staff a post-holder must manage
The scope and independence expected at each group of grades
The number of years you must have served at the grade below

questions.hint: Higher levels involve greater scope, complexity and independence.

questions.prompt: How does Making Effective Decisions typically differ at a higher level?

options.text: It involves picking the quickest option whatever the risk to delivery
It involves following set procedures without having to exercise any judgement
It involves referring every choice upwards to a manager to avoid any error
It involves weighing complex or incomplete evidence and balancing risk

questions.hint: Higher levels deal with ambiguity and consequence.

questions.prompt: What is the Leadership expectation at HEO and SEO?

options.text: Leading only on days when a senior manager is absent
Leading a team or piece of work, setting direction and developing others
Setting overall departmental strategy and speaking for the department
Following others' direction while keeping to your own tasks

questions.hint: HEO and SEO lead teams or work packages.

questions.prompt: If you write evidence at a level below the post, what is likely to happen?

options.text: You may look unready for the grade you are seeking
The panel will rescale it automatically to the grade
The advert will be amended to a lower grade
You will score extra for modesty and accuracy

questions.hint: Evidence should match the target level.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of claiming evidence from a level above the post that you have not really done?

options.text: It raises your sift score and carries no further consequence afterwards
It can fail under questioning at interview and damage your credibility
It is ignored because panels only ever score the written evidence
It is acceptable provided you attended the meetings that were involved

questions.hint: Claims must be backed by genuine experience.

questions.prompt: Which general mapping of levels to grades is correct?

options.text: SEO and Grade 7 share the lowest level of all
One separate level for each grade from AA to Grade 6
AA and AO lowest, then EO, then HEO and SEO, then Grade 7 and 6
EO and HEO share the first level and Grade 7 has the second

questions.hint: The usual pattern groups grades into levels.

questions.prompt: An EO wants to move to HEO. Which approach to behaviour evidence is most useful?

options.text: Find examples already showing HEO-level scope such as leading work
Use examples from education, since work examples are not allowed
Wait until someone formally offers a promotion before collecting any
Use only examples that show EO tasks done to a very high standard

questions.hint: Show evidence at the target level.

questions.prompt: At Grade 7, how does Leadership usually go beyond the HEO and SEO expectation?

options.text: It stops being assessed because seniority is assumed
It narrows to delivering your own tasks without direction
It shifts to supervising only a single small team
It extends to leading through other managers and across teams

questions.hint: Higher levels involve leading through others.

items.title: L11: What each selection stage assesses
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body: Selection usually follows stages, and each stage tends to assess particular Success Profile elements. A sift is the first filter, normally based on your written application: a CV, a personal statement or answers to questions, scored against a small number of criteria. Because panels may have many applications, the sift often looks only at the lead criteria. Online tests, where used, assess ability, such as numerical, verbal or situational judgement. Some roles use a technical assessment, for example a written exercise, a case study or an analysis task. The interview then explores behaviours, strengths and experience in more depth, and may include a presentation. The final stage may be a pre-employment check rather than an assessment. The principle is proportionality: assess each element once, at the stage that suits it, rather than repeating it. Candidates should expect the stages and elements to be set out in the advert, though dates can move. Scores at a stage are usually compared with a pass mark or used to rank candidates, and only those who pass or rank high enough move on. If you are invited to an interview you have passed the sift, but that does not carry forward the sift score, which is not normally added to the interview score. Plan your evidence so that you do not repeat the same example in the sift and the interview unless asked.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a sift?

options.text: To confirm that candidates hold the required clearance
To collect and verify references for shortlisted people
To filter applications against a few criteria
To make the final offer to the successful candidate

questions.hint: The sift is the first filter.

questions.prompt: Which stage most often assesses ability?

options.text: The sift of written applications and personal statements
Online tests such as numerical, verbal or situational judgement
The pre-employment check carried out after an offer has been made
The probation review held in the first months of the job

questions.hint: Ability is typically tested with online assessments.

questions.prompt: At which stage are behaviours, strengths and experience usually explored in depth?

options.text: The medical check
The advert
The reference check
The interview

questions.hint: Interviews explore these in depth.

questions.prompt: Why do recruiters generally assess each element only once?

options.text: To keep the process proportionate and avoid repetition
The law forbids repeated assessment of a candidate
Candidates are not supposed to know what is assessed
Tests are considered unreliable if repeated at interview

questions.hint: Proportionality avoids over-assessment.

questions.prompt: Why do panels often score only the lead criteria at sift?

options.text: The other criteria are legally irrelevant to the person being appointed
The interview repeats the sift in full, so nothing is lost by narrowing it
With many applications, a few criteria allow efficient and fair filtering
Candidates are only permitted to address one criterion in an application

questions.hint: A focused sift is fair and manageable.

questions.prompt: Is a candidate's sift score normally added to their interview score?

options.text: Scores are combined only at SEO and above, where posts are scarcer
Scores are always added together to give each candidate a final ranking
Scores are combined for external candidates only, not civil servants
Stages are normally assessed separately and scores are not combined

questions.hint: Stage scores are not usually combined.

questions.prompt: What does a pre-employment check usually involve?

options.text: Choosing between candidates whose scores were equal
Checking identity, right to work, references and any clearance
Re-scoring the interview in case of a close decision
Repeating the ability tests under controlled conditions

questions.hint: It confirms eligibility rather than merit.

questions.prompt: Which exercise might form a technical assessment?

options.text: A written exercise or case study linked to the work
A group social event with the existing team
A random draw among candidates who passed sift
A general personality questionnaire used for every role

questions.hint: Technical assessments test job-specific skills.

questions.prompt: You reach interview having used an example at sift. How should you prepare?

options.text: Prepare other examples too, unless asked to expand on sift evidence
Plan to repeat the sift wording exactly to stay consistent
Avoid mentioning that example in case it counts against you
Ask the panel to reread your sift answers before you speak

questions.hint: Having alternatives lets you respond flexibly.

questions.prompt: Who decides which elements are assessed at which stage?

options.text: Each applicant, by choosing which to be assessed on
The Civil Service Commission, case by case for each vacancy
The previous post-holder, who knows the job best
The recruiting department, which sets them out in the advert

questions.hint: The recruiter designs the process.

items.title: L11: Internal and external competitions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: A vacancy on Civil Service Jobs may be advertised in different ways. A competition open to all can be applied for by people from outside the Civil Service as well as civil servants. A competition open to civil servants only is restricted to people already employed in the Civil Service. Some are open to civil servants in a single department or across government. The route a department chooses reflects its needs: external advertising brings in new skills, while internal advertising can be quicker and gives staff progression. Both must still be fair and open competition on merit, because the Recruitment Principles require that. Being internal gives you some advantages, such as knowing the department and having a current manager who can support you, and some disadvantages, such as competing with colleagues you know and having the panel know you. Do not assume that being an existing member of staff gives priority, and do not assume that outsiders are favoured. In an external competition, civil servants apply on the same basis as everyone else; their existing grade does not give them extra marks. Existing civil servants often keep their continuous service when they move, while external appointees start new service, and terms can differ by department. Before applying, check the eligibility wording in the advert, because applying to a restricted competition without eligibility can waste your effort and may count as a false claim.

questions.prompt: What does a vacancy open to civil servants only mean?

options.text: Only people working in the recruiting department can apply
Only people already employed in the Civil Service can apply
Only people already holding security clearance can apply
Only people at the grade directly below the vacancy can apply

questions.hint: It restricts applications to existing civil servants.

questions.prompt: What must both internal and external competitions satisfy?

options.text: A rule that the post is offered to the longest-serving applicant
A requirement that each department chooses its own outcome
Fair and open competition on merit under the Recruitment Principles
A requirement that internal staff are always shortlisted first

questions.hint: The principles apply whatever the route.

questions.prompt: Why might a department choose external advertising?

options.text: Because internal staff are barred from applying
To bring in skills or experience not available internally
Because the law requires it for every senior post
Because it is always cheaper than internal advertising

questions.hint: External advertising widens the pool of skills.

questions.prompt: What is a typical reason to restrict a competition to civil servants?

options.text: It guarantees that a named person will be selected
It removes the need for a panel and scoring criteria
It lets the department avoid following the Recruitment Principles
It can be quicker and gives existing staff progression opportunities

questions.hint: Internal competitions can be faster and support progression.

questions.prompt: An existing civil servant applies in an open external competition. How is the application assessed?

options.text: On the same basis as every other applicant
With extra marks for the current grade
Only after external candidates have been assessed
With a lower pass mark than external applicants

questions.hint: All applicants are assessed on merit against the same criteria.

questions.prompt: Which is a potential disadvantage of being an internal candidate?

options.text: You must repeat probation whatever the new post
You lose your continuous service as soon as you apply
The panel may know you and colleagues are often applying too
You are not allowed to receive any feedback on your result

questions.hint: Familiarity and colleague competition can cut both ways.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of applying to a competition for which you are not eligible?

options.text: You gain priority consideration on later competitions because you tried
You are guaranteed a feedback conversation with the panel afterwards
You waste effort and risk a false claim if you misrepresent your eligibility
You are automatically added to a reserve list for similar posts

questions.hint: Check eligibility before applying.

questions.prompt: Which statement about continuous service when moving is most accurate?

options.text: Existing civil servants often keep continuous service, but terms can differ by department
Continuous service is a benefit that applies only to external recruits
Continuous service is always kept, with identical terms in every department
Continuous service is always lost when you move from one department to another

questions.hint: Terms can vary, so check.

questions.prompt: An advert is open to civil servants across government. Who can apply?

options.text: Anyone working anywhere in the public sector
Civil servants from any department
Only members of the Senior Civil Service
Only civil servants from the recruiting department

questions.hint: Across government means any civil servant.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether you meet a restricted competition's eligibility. What should you do?

options.text: Apply and rely on it not being checked
Assume you are eligible if your department is named anywhere
Ask a colleague who has applied before to judge for you
Check the advert wording and ask the recruiting contact or HR

questions.hint: Ask before applying.

items.title: L11: Loans, secondments and level transfers compared
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental HR policy
items.body: Three terms are often confused, so it helps to separate them precisely. A level transfer is a permanent move to a post at the same grade, usually in another team or department. It is a change of job rather than a promotion, and pay normally stays at the same level, subject to the receiving department's policy. A loan is a temporary move within the Civil Service from one department to another, normally for a fixed period, during which the person typically remains employed by the lending department while working in the host. A secondment is a temporary move that may involve another sector, such as to or from a local authority, a charity or a private company, for a fixed period, with an agreement setting out the terms. Both loans and secondments usually have a return date, a home post or a right to return, and a named line manager at the host. They are not promotions, though they can be used to build evidence for one. Because they are time limited, they typically do not count as a permanent move, and the host cannot normally make you a permanent member of staff without a separate competition. Before accepting, check who pays you, who manages performance, what happens if the host's needs change and what the return arrangements are. These practical points matter more than the label on the agreement.

questions.prompt: Which describes a level transfer?

options.text: A temporary promotion into a higher grade
A fixed-term move to an organisation outside government
A permanent move to a post at the same grade
A change of pay band within your current post

questions.hint: Level transfers move you sideways at grade.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to pay on a level transfer?

options.text: It normally stays at the same level, subject to the receiving department's policy
It rises by a fixed percentage set across government for all level transfers
It drops to the bottom of the receiving department's pay range
It is renegotiated from scratch whatever the person earned before

questions.hint: A same-grade move is not a pay rise.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a loan?

options.text: A permanent exit from the lending department
A temporary move between departments for a fixed period
A promotion made at the host's request
A permanent move to a different grade in the host

questions.hint: A loan is a fixed-period move within the Civil Service.

questions.prompt: How does a secondment differ from a loan?

options.text: A secondment never has a defined return date
A secondment is always unpaid for the person moving
A secondment is always permanent once the period passes
A secondment may cross sectors, with terms in an agreement

questions.hint: Secondments can cross sectors.

questions.prompt: Who usually employs a person on loan during the loan?

options.text: An external recruitment agency
The host department in every case
The Civil Service Commission
The lending department

questions.hint: The person usually stays employed by the lender.

questions.prompt: Can a host department simply make someone on loan a permanent member of staff?

options.text: Not without a separate fair and open competition
It can once the person has completed six months in the host post
It can if the host manager simply asks the lender to agree
It can if the person's pay is lower than the host grade

questions.hint: Permanent appointment needs a competition.

questions.prompt: Which question about a loan or secondment matters most before accepting?

options.text: How large the host's office is and which floor it occupies
Whether the host's logo appears on your pass
Who pays you, who manages performance and how you return
Which of the host's teams are the most senior

questions.hint: Practical terms decide the value of the move.

questions.prompt: Are loans and secondments promotions?

options.text: They always carry a pay rise from the first day
Not in themselves, though they can build promotion evidence
They replace your substantive grade for the duration
They always lead to a promotion at the end of the period

questions.hint: They are temporary arrangements.

questions.prompt: Why is a time-limited move relevant to a promotion case?

options.text: It resets your appraisal rating to the highest level for the next year
It guarantees you a pass at sift in every later competition you enter
It can give new evidence of skills and breadth at or above your grade
It lets you skip the interview stage in the next competition you enter

questions.hint: It supplies evidence, not entitlement.

questions.prompt: An agreement sets out a return date and a host line manager. What does it most likely cover?

options.text: A permanent level transfer
A loan or secondment
A reasonable adjustment plan
A promotion board decision

questions.hint: These are typical elements of a temporary-move agreement.

items.title: L11: Temporary promotion and acting up basics
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Recruitment Principles
items.body: A temporary promotion, or acting up, means doing the job of a higher grade for a period while your substantive grade remains the same. It is often used to cover a vacancy, a maternity leave, a secondment or a surge of work. In many departments, the person receives higher pay for the duration, but practice varies, so check your department's policy. The period is usually fixed, and the person normally returns to their substantive post when it ends unless they win a permanent post in a competition. Acting up can be valuable: it gives you experience, evidence for a promotion application and a chance to test whether you enjoy the role. It carries risks too. If the arrangement is informal, there may be no extra pay, no clear end date and no recognition. If the arrangement is long, others may feel excluded, which raises fairness questions, and the Recruitment Principles expect departments to avoid using temporary arrangements as a back door to permanent promotion. A temporary promotion does not create a right to the permanent role, and the permanent post must be filled by fair and open competition. Before agreeing, ask how you will be selected, how long it will last, what pay applies, what support you will receive and what happens at the end. Keep a record of what you achieve, because it will form your evidence later.

questions.prompt: In Civil Service usage, what is meant by acting up?

options.text: Doing the job of a higher grade for a period while keeping your substantive grade
Moving to another department at your current grade for a short time
Taking unpaid leave to work for an outside organisation
Being permanently promoted into the higher post without a competition

questions.hint: Temporary promotion covers higher duties.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to an acting-up person when the period ends?

options.text: They leave the Civil Service once the temporary period is complete
They stay in the higher post automatically unless a manager objects
They are moved to another department at the same higher grade
They return to their substantive post unless they win a permanent role

questions.hint: The arrangement is temporary.

questions.prompt: Does acting up create a right to the permanent role?

options.text: It does not, because permanent posts must be filled by fair and open competition
It does when the line manager agrees in writing that the post is theirs
It does when the person's evidence in the acting role is strong enough
It does once the person has acted up for a set number of months in post

questions.hint: Acting up does not create entitlement.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of an informal acting-up arrangement?

options.text: A rule barring you from applying for the permanent post
A guaranteed pay increase that cannot later be reversed
There may be no clear end date, pay or recognition
A break in your continuous service

questions.hint: Informal arrangements are often vague.

questions.prompt: Why can long acting-up arrangements raise fairness concerns?

options.text: They prevent the acting person from taking annual leave or training
They always cost the department more than running a competition would
They become unlawful once they have run for longer than a single week
Other eligible staff may not have had the chance to gain the same experience

questions.hint: Fairness requires access to opportunities.

questions.prompt: Which question should you ask before agreeing to act up?

options.text: Whether you may keep the acting grade if you later decline the permanent role
How you were selected, how long it lasts, what pay applies and what support is offered
Whether the manager already has a preferred person in mind for the permanent post
Whether the permanent post will be given to you once the acting period ends

questions.hint: These terms determine the value of the move.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of acting up for a promotion application?

options.text: It lets you skip the sift
It means no interview is needed later
It gives you a permanent pay rise
It provides evidence at the higher grade

questions.hint: Evidence is the benefit.

questions.prompt: How does pay usually work while acting up?

options.text: Pay is always replaced by time off in lieu of a higher salary
Pay is always unchanged from your substantive grade for the whole period
Often higher pay for the period, but practice varies by department
Pay is always doubled compared with your usual salary for the duration

questions.hint: Check departmental policy.

questions.prompt: What should you do to benefit from acting-up experience later?

options.text: Keep a running record of your achievements as you go
Avoid recording anything so you appear modest
Rely on your manager's memory of your work
Wait until the end to recall what happened

questions.hint: A running record helps later.

questions.prompt: Which arrangement reflects good practice?

options.text: A hand-picked successor kept in post for years with no competition
A fixed end date, a clear selection method and an early advert for the permanent post
An open-ended arrangement with no review points or planned end date
An arrangement kept confidential from the rest of the team and other grades

questions.hint: Good practice is time-limited and transparent.

items.title: L11: Merit, fair and open competition
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles; Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010
items.body: The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010 put the Civil Service on a statutory footing and requires that selection for appointment to the Civil Service is on merit on the basis of fair and open competition. The Civil Service Commission publishes the Recruitment Principles that explain how to apply this. Merit means appointing the best available person for the job, judged against the requirements of the post. Fair means that all candidates are treated equally and assessed against the same criteria with no unjustified advantage or disadvantage. Open means that potential candidates have a reasonable opportunity to find out about vacancies and to apply, which is why vacancies are normally advertised. The Principles also expect that selection processes are transparent, proportionate and based on criteria, that there are records of decisions and that candidates can ask for feedback. Departments should have a way for candidates to raise complaints. The Principles allow some exceptions, such as short-term appointments and certain schemes, and these are narrow. The phrase best available person matters: a panel may appoint someone who is not outstanding if no one else meets the standard, but it may not appoint someone who does not meet the criteria. Merit is not seniority, and being known to the panel is not a criterion. Anyone in recruitment should be able to explain each decision using the stated criteria and the evidence recorded.

questions.prompt: What does merit mean under the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: Appointing the best available person judged against the requirements of the post
Appointing the longest-serving applicant who has applied for the post
Appointing the candidate who is best known to members of the panel
Appointing the candidate whose appointment would cost the department least

questions.hint: Merit is about the best person for the job.

questions.prompt: What does fair mean in this context?

options.text: Panels may decide without set criteria
All candidates receive equal marks whatever their evidence
Existing staff are always favoured over outside applicants
All candidates are treated equally against the same criteria

questions.hint: Fairness means equal treatment against criteria.

questions.prompt: In the Recruitment Principles, what does the word open mean?

options.text: Every decision is published with the names and scores of all candidates
Potential candidates have a reasonable opportunity to find out about vacancies and apply
Every vacancy is first offered to internal staff before outside applicants
Every applicant who meets the minimum criteria is guaranteed an interview

questions.hint: Open means accessible opportunity.

questions.prompt: Which Act requires selection on merit by fair and open competition?

options.text: The Civil Service Act 1946, which set up the original grading structure
The Data Protection Act 2018, which governs personal information
The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010
The Official Secrets Act 1989, which governs unauthorised disclosures

questions.hint: The 2010 Act sets the statutory requirement.

questions.prompt: Who publishes the Recruitment Principles?

options.text: The Cabinet Secretary's private office
The National Audit Office
The Civil Service Commission
Each department separately without any central oversight

questions.hint: The Commission publishes them.

questions.prompt: May a panel appoint someone who does not meet the criteria because no one else applied?

options.text: It may when the line manager asks for it
Appointees must meet the requirements of the post
It may when the panel feels it is practical to do so
It may when the person is already a civil servant

questions.hint: Merit requires the person to meet the standard.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a proper basis for a merit decision?

options.text: Evidence against the person specification
Performance at the assessments
Meeting the requirements of the post
Being known to members of the panel

questions.hint: Familiarity is not merit.

questions.prompt: What should a department be able to do after each selection decision?

options.text: Explain it using the stated criteria and the recorded evidence
Refuse requests for feedback, since the decision is final once recorded
Explain it by reference to each candidate's seniority and length of service
Destroy the interview notes once the decision is made so they cannot be misread

questions.hint: Decisions should be explainable.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase best available person allow?

options.text: Setting the criteria aside after the interviews
Appointing someone below the standard when time is short
Appointing the strongest candidate who meets the standard
Appointing anyone who happens to be free to start

questions.hint: Standards still apply.

questions.prompt: Why are vacancies normally advertised?

options.text: To reduce the number of applications received
To raise the profile of the recruiting department
To satisfy a tax rule on recruitment spend
To meet the openness part of the principle

questions.hint: Advertising gives a reasonable opportunity to apply.

items.title: L11: The role of the Civil Service Commission
items.source: Civil Service Commission; Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010
items.body: The Civil Service Commission is an independent body established on a statutory basis by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. It has two main roles that matter to job applicants. First, it sets and publishes the Recruitment Principles and oversees that appointments are made on merit through fair and open competition. It approves the exceptions to that rule and monitors departments through audits and reporting. Second, it considers complaints under the Recruitment Principles and, separately, under the Civil Service Code. A person who believes there has been a breach of the Recruitment Principles should normally raise the concern first with the department, using its complaints process. If they remain dissatisfied after the department has responded, they may bring the complaint to the Commission, usually within a limited time. The Commission looks at whether the Principles were breached, not at whether it would have scored the candidate differently, and it does not generally re-run an assessment. It can make recommendations to departments. It also hears concerns raised by civil servants under the Civil Service Code. Its independence means it is not part of any department and reports to Parliament. The Commission is not a general appeals body for people who failed an interview, and a complaint needs to identify a specific breach, such as an unfair process or an unadvertised vacancy.

questions.prompt: What is the Civil Service Commission?

options.text: An independent body set up by statute to oversee recruitment principles
A private recruitment agency that departments hire to run competitions
A trade union that represents senior civil servants in pay talks
A department of the Cabinet Office led by a minister of state

questions.hint: It is statutory and independent.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate normally do before complaining to the Commission?

options.text: Wait for the Commission to make contact with you about the competition
Raise the concern with the department through its complaints process
Post the concern publicly so that the department is pressed to respond quickly
Ask a minister to intervene directly in the outcome of the competition

questions.hint: Departmental routes come first.

questions.prompt: What does the Commission examine in a recruitment complaint?

options.text: Whether it would have scored the candidate higher
Whether the Recruitment Principles were breached
Whether the panel liked the candidate
Whether the candidate was a better fit than the winner

questions.hint: It examines breaches of principles.

questions.prompt: Does the Commission generally re-run an assessment?

options.text: It re-runs an assessment when the candidate has asked for it twice
It re-runs every assessment that a candidate complains about in full
It looks at whether the principles were breached rather than re-scoring candidates
It re-runs assessments for small departments that lack HR capacity

questions.hint: It does not re-score candidates.

questions.prompt: Which concern would the Commission consider?

options.text: A dislike of the interview room or the time of day it was held
A view that the winning candidate was personally less likeable
A disagreement with the panel over a mark of five rather than six
A post filled without advert where the Principles required one

questions.hint: A specific breach of the Principles.

questions.prompt: What can the Commission do after finding a breach?

options.text: Make recommendations to the department
Set the candidate's salary on appointment
Appoint the complaining candidate directly
Dismiss the panel members involved

questions.hint: It recommends rather than directs.

questions.prompt: What other role does the Commission have besides recruitment oversight?

options.text: Running the civil service pension scheme and paying benefits to members
Appointing government ministers and advising on their responsibilities
Setting civil service pay awards and negotiating them with the unions
Hearing concerns raised under the Civil Service Code

questions.hint: It hears Code concerns.

questions.prompt: Why does the Commission's independence from departments matter?

options.text: It means the Commission has no formal rules of its own
It removes the need for any Recruitment Principles
It allows impartial oversight of recruitment decisions
It lets the Commission run each department's recruitment itself

questions.hint: Independence supports credibility.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the Commission?

options.text: It is not a general appeals body for people who failed an interview
It sits inside each department and reports to its permanent secretary
It overturns a rejected candidate's result on request
It writes and edits job adverts for departments

questions.hint: It deals with breaches, not general appeals.

questions.prompt: Which Act gave the Commission its statutory footing?

options.text: The Civil Service Pensions Act 1972, which governs pension arrangements
The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010
The Freedom of Information Act 2000, which governs access to information
The Public Records Act 1958, which governs the preservation of records

questions.hint: The 2010 Act.

items.title: L11: Building a case for promotion
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; departmental talent guidance
items.body: A promotion case rests on evidence that you already operate at the next grade, not on time served or hopes. Start by reading the Success Profile for the target grade: its behaviour level, typical scope and any technical requirements. Then compare your current evidence honestly. Where you are strong, gather specific examples with outcomes, and where you are weak, seek stretch work, a loan or a period of acting up that supplies it. Keep a running evidence log: situation, what you did, the result, the date and who can verify it. Ask your line manager for regular feedback and request their view of whether you are ready. Ask a senior colleague to act as a sponsor or mentor, someone who can introduce you to opportunities, give honest feedback and describe your work to others. Be visible: share outcomes in team meetings and in your appraisal. Use appraisal and development conversations to agree objectives that stretch you towards the next grade. Remember that in the Civil Service a promotion is gained through fair and open competition, so your line manager cannot simply promote you; the best they can do is support your readiness and tell you when a suitable vacancy appears. Apply when you can evidence the higher-grade criteria, even if you do not feel fully ready, because a panel judges evidence rather than confidence.

questions.prompt: What should a promotion case primarily rest on?

options.text: Your length of service at the current grade
A manager's promise that a post will be found
Your wish for a higher salary
Evidence that you already operate at the next grade

questions.hint: Evidence against criteria is what counts.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in building a case for promotion?

options.text: Apply at once to see how you score
Read the Success Profile for the target grade
Ask your manager to confirm a pay rise
Move department to find a bigger team

questions.hint: Know the standard first.

questions.prompt: What should an evidence log contain?

options.text: The situation, what you did, the result, the date and who can verify it
The opinions of colleagues about your personality and working style
A list of the awards and honours you hope to win in future
Only your job titles and the dates on which you held each of them

questions.hint: A log should be specific and verifiable.

questions.prompt: You have a gap against the target grade. What is a good response?

options.text: Apply and hope the panel overlooks the missing evidence at sift
Wait for the gap to close by itself as you gain more years of service
Seek stretch work, a loan or acting up that supplies the missing evidence
Ignore the gap and write around it in every application you make

questions.hint: Create opportunities to fill it.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a sponsor or mentor in building a case?

options.text: Writing your application and sift statement for you to save you time
Giving honest feedback, introducing opportunities and describing your work to others
Confirming your pay band and start date in the promoted post before the competition
Deciding your result at interview by speaking to the panel chair on your behalf

questions.hint: A sponsor helps open doors.

questions.prompt: Can a line manager simply promote you if they believe you are ready?

options.text: Promotion is by fair and open competition, so they cannot
They can if the department is small
They can if the post is currently vacant
They can if you have already acted up in the role

questions.hint: Competition is required.

questions.prompt: What can a line manager legitimately do to support your promotion?

options.text: Promise you a particular result if you apply for the next vacancy
Pre-select you for a post before it has been advertised to everyone
Support your readiness, give feedback and tell you about suitable vacancies
Adjust your sift score before the panel sees your application

questions.hint: Support is allowed; pre-selection is not.

questions.prompt: Why should you apply when you can evidence the criteria, even if you do not feel fully ready?

options.text: Applications are valid only once in your career
Seniority decides between close candidates
Confidence is the decisive criterion at interview
Panels judge evidence rather than confidence

questions.hint: Evidence is what is scored.

questions.prompt: How can appraisal conversations help your case?

options.text: By setting the pay you will receive in your next role
By agreeing objectives that stretch you towards the next grade
By securing you a promotion without the need to go through a competition
By replacing the need for an evidence log or any written record

questions.hint: Stretch objectives build evidence.

questions.prompt: Which action builds visibility without breaching any rules?

options.text: Asking an insider for the interview questions in advance
Publicly complaining about the competition process
Sharing outcomes in team meetings and appraisals
Lobbying panel members privately before the interview

questions.hint: Visibility should be legitimate.

items.title: L11: Handling feedback and setbacks
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; departmental recruitment practice
items.body: Most unsuccessful candidates can request feedback, and it is one of the best tools for improving. The advert or the outcome email normally says how to ask, and departments usually offer a written or verbal summary of how you scored against the criteria. Ask promptly, because feedback is easier for the panel to give when the process is recent, and prepare questions in advance: which criteria cost you marks, what a stronger answer would have contained and how close you were to the pass mark. Listen without arguing. Feedback is about your evidence on the day, not your worth. Separate what you can change, such as the way you structured examples, from what you cannot, such as strong competition. Write down the points and look for patterns across several applications. If the feedback is brief or unclear, ask a polite follow-up question. If you think it reveals unfairness, such as irrelevant questions or inconsistent scoring, use the department's complaints route rather than arguing with the panel. Avoid contacting panel members informally, which may breach confidentiality and damage your reputation. Look after your confidence: rejection is common, particularly at HEO and above where many strong candidates compete. Turn feedback into one or two specific actions, and set a date for the next application. A reserve list place is also a positive outcome: you met the standard and may be offered a post later.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to request feedback?

options.text: Promptly after the outcome, while the process is recent
Only after you have made a formal complaint about the competition
Before you attend the interview, so you can prepare in advance
A year later, when you have gained more perspective on the process

questions.hint: Prompt requests are easier to answer.

questions.prompt: Which question is most useful in a feedback conversation?

options.text: Who else applied for the post and what each of them scored in each stage
Whether anyone on the panel was biased against me personally at the interview
Why the winning candidate was chosen in preference to me and what they said
Which criteria cost me marks and what would a stronger answer have contained

questions.hint: Focus on your evidence and improvement.

questions.prompt: What is the right attitude when you receive feedback?

options.text: Dispute each mark as it is given
Set it aside as only one person's view
Ask for a re-score during the call
Listen and note points without arguing

questions.hint: Feedback is a development tool.

questions.prompt: Why look for patterns across several applications?

options.text: Patterns prove that the panels are biased against you over time
Repeated points show where your real development need lies
Patterns show that you should stop applying for promotion posts
Patterns are irrelevant because every panel marks differently

questions.hint: Patterns show consistent issues.

questions.prompt: You believe feedback reveals unfairness. What is the proper route?

options.text: Phoning panel members to challenge them
Waiting and applying again without comment
The department's complaints process
Posting your concerns on social media

questions.hint: Use formal routes.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid contacting panel members informally after a rejection?

options.text: It may breach confidentiality and damage your reputation
It cancels your application on file automatically
It is a criminal offence in every case
Panel members are prohibited from speaking to anyone

questions.hint: Use official channels.

questions.prompt: What does a reserve list place mean?

options.text: You failed the process but are allowed to re-sit it at a later date
You have a guaranteed offer in writing for the next vacancy
You are barred from reapplying for a year after a reserve placement
You met the standard and may be offered a post later

questions.hint: Reserve means passed, no post yet.

questions.prompt: What is a useful way to turn feedback into action?

options.text: Choose one or two specific actions and set a date for the next application
Memorise the panel's wording to repeat in future answers
Wait for a new advert to appear before reflecting on the feedback at all
Change every aspect of your approach at once before the next application

questions.hint: Specific actions work best.

questions.prompt: What should you do if feedback is vague?

options.text: Make a formal complaint straight away
Ask a polite follow-up question to clarify
Withdraw from future competitions
Conclude the panel is hiding something

questions.hint: Seek clarity first.

questions.prompt: Why separate what you can change from what you cannot?

options.text: It proves the competition was unfair
It improves your pay on re-application
It focuses effort where it makes a difference
It lets you ignore all the feedback you disagree with

questions.hint: Focus on controllable factors.
